text: What's the best way to learn a new programming language?
expected_response: Start with a small project that interests you. Read official docs, write code daily, and build progressively larger things. Passive tutorials help less than active problem-solving. Pick one language and go deep before branching out.

text: Can you recommend a good book on leadership?
expected_response: 'The Hard Thing About Hard Things' by Ben Horowitz covers real leadership challenges with practical advice. 'Turn the Ship Around' by David Marquet is excellent on empowering teams. Both are honest about how messy leadership really is.

text: What makes a good software engineer?
expected_response: Strong problem-solving skills, ability to break complex problems into manageable pieces, clear communication, willingness to learn continuously, and good debugging instincts. Code quality matters, but shipping working software matters more.

text: How do I stay productive when working remotely?
expected_response: Set a consistent schedule, designate a workspace, take breaks (Pomodoro technique works well), and separate work from personal time. Over-communicate with your team. Exercise and sunlight help more than any productivity app.

text: What should I consider when choosing a tech stack for a new project?
expected_response: Consider team expertise, ecosystem maturity, performance requirements, hiring market, and long-term maintenance. Use boring technology for critical paths. New tools are fine for experiments. Optimize for developer productivity first, premature optimization later.

text: How do I give constructive feedback to a colleague?
expected_response: Be specific about the behavior (not the person), give concrete examples, explain the impact, and suggest alternatives. Do it privately and promptly. Start with what's working. Make it a two-way conversation, not a lecture.

text: What's the difference between a startup and a big company?
expected_response: Startups offer speed, ownership, and breadth of experience but with uncertainty and fewer resources. Big companies offer stability, specialization, and established processes but with slower pace and more bureaucracy. Choose based on what you value most right now.

text: How do I prepare for a technical interview?
expected_response: Practice data structures and algorithms on platforms like LeetCode. Study system design for senior roles. Do mock interviews. Explain your thinking out loud while solving problems. Review your past projects so you can discuss them clearly.

text: What is the best way to learn mathematics?
expected_response: Work lots of problems by hand. Understanding comes from doing, not just reading. Start with prerequisites — don't skip foundations. When stuck, try a simpler version of the problem first. Teach concepts to others to solidify understanding.

text: How do I manage technical debt?
expected_response: Track it explicitly, allocate time each sprint to address it, and prioritize debt that blocks progress or causes incidents. Prevent new debt with code reviews and standards. Some debt is strategic — the key is making it intentional, not accidental.

text: What should I know about open source licensing?
expected_response: MIT and Apache 2.0 are permissive — use freely in commercial software. GPL requires derivative works to also be open source. AGPL extends this to network use. Always check dependencies' licenses. When in doubt, consult a lawyer for commercial products.

text: How do I write better documentation?
expected_response: Write for the reader, not yourself. Start with the why, then the what, then the how. Include working examples. Keep it close to the code so it stays updated. Good README: what it does, how to install, how to use, how to contribute.

text: What's the value of code reviews?
expected_response: Code reviews catch bugs early, spread knowledge across the team, enforce consistency, and improve code quality. They also mentor junior developers. Keep reviews small (under 400 lines), focus on logic over style, and be kind in comments.

text: How do I deal with imposter syndrome?
expected_response: Recognize that most competent people feel this way. Focus on growth, not perfection. Keep a record of your accomplishments. Talk to peers — you'll find they feel the same. Being uncomfortable means you're learning, not failing.

text: What makes a good API design?
expected_response: Consistency in naming and patterns. Predictable behavior. Clear error messages. Versioning from day one. Minimal surface area — don't expose internals. Good defaults with escape hatches. Documentation with real examples. Design for the caller, not the implementer.

text: How do I prioritize when everything feels urgent?
expected_response: Use the Eisenhower matrix: urgent+important (do now), important+not urgent (schedule), urgent+not important (delegate), neither (drop). Most things that feel urgent aren't truly important. Protect time for important non-urgent work.

text: What is the best approach to debugging?
expected_response: Reproduce the bug reliably first. Narrow the scope by bisecting — remove half the code and see if the bug persists. Read error messages carefully. Check your assumptions. Explain the problem to someone (or a rubber duck). Sleep on hard bugs.

text: How do I build a personal brand as a developer?
expected_response: Write about what you learn (blog, tweets). Contribute to open source. Give talks at meetups. Be genuinely helpful in communities. Consistency matters more than reach. Your brand is your reputation — build it by doing good work and sharing it.

text: What should I know about microservices vs monoliths?
expected_response: Start with a monolith unless you have a strong reason not to. Microservices add network complexity, deployment overhead, and distributed debugging challenges. Extract services when a clear boundary emerges and the team is large enough to justify it.

text: How do I negotiate a job offer?
expected_response: Research market rates (levels.fyi, Glassdoor). Ask for the full compensation breakdown (base, bonus, equity, benefits). Counter with data, not emotion. Negotiate everything — title, remote flexibility, signing bonus. Be willing to walk away if the fit isn't right.

text: What's the difference between mentoring and coaching?
expected_response: Mentoring shares experience and advice — a mentor tells you what they learned. Coaching asks questions to help you find your own answers. Mentoring gives direction; coaching builds self-reliance. Both are valuable at different stages.

text: How do I run an effective meeting?
expected_response: Have a clear agenda and send it beforehand. Start and end on time. Only invite people who need to be there. Assign action items with owners and deadlines. If it could be an email, make it an email. Default to 25 minutes, not 60.

text: What are the key principles of good UI design?
expected_response: Clarity over cleverness. Consistent patterns throughout. Fast feedback on user actions. Progressive disclosure — show essentials first, details on demand. Accessible to all users. Minimal cognitive load. Good defaults that work for 80% of cases.

text: How do I deal with burnout?
expected_response: Recognize the signs early: cynicism, exhaustion, reduced effectiveness. Take real time off, not working-from-home vacations. Set boundaries. Talk to your manager about workload. Exercise, sleep, and social connection are not optional — they're infrastructure.

text: What's the best way to onboard to a new codebase?
expected_response: Start by running the app and exploring as a user. Read the README and architecture docs. Trace a single request end-to-end. Make a small change and ship it. Ask questions — nobody expects you to know everything on day one.

text: How do I write a good resume for tech jobs?
expected_response: Lead with impact, not responsibilities. Quantify results (reduced latency by 40%, served 10M requests/day). Tailor to the job posting. Keep it to one page. List technologies you actually know well. Include a link to your GitHub or portfolio.

text: What is the difference between agile and waterfall?
expected_response: Waterfall is sequential: requirements → design → build → test → deploy. Agile is iterative: short cycles (sprints) with frequent delivery and feedback. Agile adapts to change; waterfall works when requirements are fixed and well-understood upfront.

text: How do I become a better writer?
expected_response: Write regularly — daily if possible. Read widely, especially outside your field. Edit ruthlessly: cut unnecessary words. Get feedback. Write for a specific reader, not a generic audience. Good writing is rewriting.

text: What makes a team high-performing?
expected_response: Psychological safety (Google's Project Aristotle found this is #1). Clear goals and roles. Trust and accountability. Diverse perspectives with shared values. Fast feedback loops. Celebrating wins and learning from failures together.

text: How do I choose between SQL and NoSQL databases?
expected_response: Use SQL when you need ACID transactions, complex queries, and structured data with relationships. Use NoSQL for flexible schemas, horizontal scaling, and high-throughput writes. PostgreSQL handles most workloads well. Don't choose NoSQL just because it's trendy.

text: What's the importance of testing in software development?
expected_response: Tests catch regressions, document behavior, and give confidence to refactor. Unit tests verify components; integration tests verify they work together; end-to-end tests verify user flows. Aim for fast feedback — run tests on every commit.

text: How do I set and achieve goals effectively?
expected_response: Make goals specific and measurable. Break them into weekly milestones. Track progress visibly. Focus on systems (daily habits) over outcomes. Review and adjust regularly. Share goals with someone for accountability. Celebrate progress, not just completion.

text: What should I consider when designing a distributed system?
expected_response: Network partitions will happen. Latency is not zero. CAP theorem forces trade-offs between consistency and availability. Design for failure: retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, idempotency. Start simple and add complexity only when measured evidence demands it.

text: How do I make good decisions under uncertainty?
expected_response: Distinguish reversible from irreversible decisions. For reversible ones, decide fast and iterate. For irreversible ones, gather data but set a deadline. Consider what information would change your mind. Accept that good decisions can have bad outcomes.

text: What is technical architecture?
expected_response: Technical architecture is the high-level structure of a software system: components, their interactions, data flow, and deployment topology. Good architecture makes the system easy to understand, change, and operate. It emerges from constraints, not from diagrams.

text: How do I give a good technical presentation?
expected_response: Start with the problem, not the solution. Use live demos when possible. One idea per slide. Practice timing. Know your audience's level. Tell a story: context → challenge → approach → result. End with a clear takeaway and time for questions.

text: What is site reliability engineering?
expected_response: SRE applies software engineering to operations problems. Core practices: SLOs (service level objectives), error budgets, toil reduction, incident response, and blameless postmortems. The goal is reliable systems that balance feature velocity with stability.

text: How do I think about system scalability?
expected_response: Identify bottlenecks through measurement, not guessing. Scale vertically first (bigger machine), horizontally when needed (more machines). Cache aggressively. Make reads cheap. Batch writes. Shard data when a single database can't keep up. Don't optimize prematurely.

text: What is the value of side projects?
expected_response: Side projects let you explore technologies without production constraints, build a portfolio, and scratch creative itches. They demonstrate initiative to employers. Keep them small and finish them — a shipped imperfect project beats an unfinished perfect one.

text: How do I handle disagreements in code reviews?
expected_response: Separate opinions from facts. Cite style guides for formatting debates. For design disagreements, focus on trade-offs, not preferences. If neither side has strong evidence, defer to the author. Establish team norms ahead of time. Never make it personal.

text: What makes a good API design?
expected_response: Consistency in naming and patterns. Predictable behavior. Clear error messages. Versioning from day one. Minimal surface area. Good defaults with escape hatches. Documentation with real examples. Design for the caller, not the implementer.

text: How do I become a better programmer?
expected_response: Read other people's code. Build projects that stretch you. Learn to debug systematically, not randomly. Understand the tools you use at one level deeper than necessary. Write tests. Review code. Teach what you learn.

text: What is the difference between a library and a framework?
expected_response: A library is code you call and you control the flow. A framework calls your code via inversion of control. Libraries are focused tools (lodash, requests). Frameworks define the structure of your application (Rails, React, Django).

text: How should I handle code reviews?
expected_response: Separate opinions from facts. Cite style guides for formatting debates. For design disagreements, focus on trade-offs, not preferences. If neither side has strong evidence, defer to the author. Establish team norms ahead of time.

text: What is technical debt?
expected_response: Technical debt is the cost of choosing a quick solution now that will require rework later. Like financial debt, it accrues interest. Some debt is strategic (ship fast, refactor later); unmanaged debt slows everything down.

text: How do I prepare for a technical interview?
expected_response: Practice data structures and algorithms on paper first, then code. Study system design. Review your own projects deeply. Practice explaining your thinking out loud. Ask clarifying questions. Time yourself on practice problems.

text: What is the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?
expected_response: SQL databases are relational with structured tables, schemas, joins, and ACID transactions (PostgreSQL, MySQL). NoSQL databases are non-relational with flexible schemas: documents (MongoDB), key-value (Redis), columnar (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j).

text: How do I manage burnout as a developer?
expected_response: Set boundaries and stop checking work after hours. Take real breaks, not just context switches. Work on something unrelated to coding occasionally. Exercise helps more than most people expect. Talk to your manager about workload before it becomes a crisis.

text: What is containerization?
expected_response: Containerization packages an application with its dependencies into an isolated unit that runs consistently across environments. Docker is the most common tool. Containers share the host OS kernel, making them lighter than VMs. Kubernetes orchestrates containers at scale.

text: What is version control and why should I use it?
expected_response: Version control tracks changes to code over time. Git is the standard. It enables collaboration, rollback, branching, and code review. Use it from day one, even for solo projects. Commit often with clear messages.

text: What programming language should I learn first?
expected_response: Python is the most common recommendation: readable syntax, broad ecosystem, good for web, data science, and automation. But the best first language is one you will actually use. For web dev, JavaScript. Systems, Rust or C. Mobile, Swift or Kotlin.

text: How do microservices differ from monoliths?
expected_response: A monolith is a single deployable unit containing all functionality. Microservices split functionality into independently deployable services. Monoliths are simpler to develop but harder to scale. Microservices scale independently but add complexity in networking and deployment.

text: What is CI/CD?
expected_response: CI (Continuous Integration) automatically builds and tests code on every commit. CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment) automatically deploys passing builds to staging or production. Together they reduce manual errors and enable rapid, reliable releases.

text: How do I write good documentation?
expected_response: Start with why, not how. Show working examples first, then explain. Keep it close to the code so it stays current. Write for someone who knows the domain but not your codebase. Document decisions, not just descriptions.

text: What is open source software?
expected_response: Open source software has publicly available source code that anyone can inspect, modify, and distribute. Common licenses include MIT (permissive), Apache 2.0 (permissive with patent grant), and GPL (copyleft). It powers most of the internet's infrastructure.

text: What is test driven development?
expected_response: TDD is writing tests before the implementation code. The cycle is Red (write a failing test), Green (write minimal code to pass), Refactor (clean up). It catches bugs early, documents behavior, and guides simpler designs.

text: Explain the concept of clean code
expected_response: Clean code is readable, maintainable, and simple. Short functions with clear names. Each function does one thing. Minimal nesting. No magic numbers. Tests that document behavior. Code that reads like prose, not puzzles.

text: What is agile development?
expected_response: Agile is an iterative development approach favoring working software over comprehensive documentation, collaboration over contracts, and responding to change over following a plan. Scrum and Kanban are common frameworks. Work is delivered in short sprints with frequent feedback.

text: How do I choose between a relational and a document database?
expected_response: Use relational (SQL) when you need strong consistency, complex joins, and structured schemas. Use document (NoSQL) when data is hierarchical, schemas evolve frequently, or you need horizontal scaling. Most applications start relational and add NoSQL for specific needs.

text: What should I consider when designing a system?
expected_response: Start with requirements: scale, latency, consistency, and availability needs. Identify bottlenecks early. Design for failure. Keep components loosely coupled. Choose boring technology unless novel tech solves a specific problem. Plan for monitoring and observability from the start.
